utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, counsel. Good afternoon, deputies. Good afternoon, everyone in the translation booths. As soon as the accused come in, we'll begin our Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the accused, and you may take your seats. As you all know, we're here for another Status Conference, and we last had one on the 20th of July and we hope we'll make progress toward moving the case ready for trial. Registrar, would you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-98-34-PT, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask the parties now, the counsel for the parties, if they'll announce their appearances. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good afternoon. My name is Franck Terrier. Today is the last time where I will appear in this courtroom, because later on I will be replaced by Kenneth Scott, who is sitting on my right. He is a senior trial attorney. I would like to inform you of that fact; I also would like to inform counsel for the Defence and the accused. This afternoon, the Prosecution is also represented by Douglas Stringer, Vassily Poriouvaev, Roeland Bos, and Manuel Bouwknecht.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We regret this is your last appearance, Mr. Terrier, we will miss you. We welcome Mr. Scott to your ranks. If Defence counsel would announce their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Kresimir Krsnik, a member of the bar association of Croatia, and Ms. Visnja Drenski Lasan is my assistant today. She is also a member of the bar association of Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Branko Seric, Defence counsel for Mr. Naletilic. I'm also a member of the bar association of Croatia, and Mr. Zelimir Par will assist me in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. I think we will pick up where we left off last time and see if we can make further some progress toward going to trial. Now, the Scheduling Order that I gave you contained a proposed set of dates that would govern the 65 ter filings, along with any other motions for judicial notice, depositions, et cetera. I recognise that Mr. Terrier's departure from the Prosecution may provide -- perhaps not, but it may provide some justification for some movement on that. I would be interested to know initially, whether or not the Prosecution feels that it could meet its responsibilities by that proposed date or would need some extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my departure will change nothing in the preparation of this case. It will go on as it has started, and I don't believe that the Prosecution in this case will ask any change in the schedule or any postponement. We are not going to be responsible for any delay in the pre-trial management of this case. Therefore, the Prosecution is in a position, and will be in a position to meet all its obligations as defined in the document sent to us. We will not ask for any delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's good news, Mr. Terrier. Thank you. The second point I would like to make is that I have been disappointed by the filings of Mr. Naletilic's counsel in the sense that he was not up to the point that I know about presently, able to make any virtually any concession in terms of facts that would not be disputed. I think in that regard that you should be aware, Mr. Krsnik, that regardless of whether or not you are willing to concede any point, no matter how peripheral or no matter how well-established, that we do intend to go right ahead with our preparations for the trial. And in that regard, I assume that the Prosecution will avail itself of whatever tools are in the Rules, such as motions for judicial notice, 95 ter affidavits, depositions, to move the proceedings along. And I also hope that Mr. Krsnik, you will perhaps reconsider your inability to admit any of the facts that the Prosecution has laid out in the document that they filed with us. I might also say in this regard that reading over all the material that we have so far, it strikes me, based upon the experience I have had with would other trials, at least one and perhaps two of which I think Mr. Stringer here is familiar with, that this particular trial insofar as the Prosecution has told us, at least it told us last time that it thought it would have somewhere in the vicinity, could not be held bound, I understand that, but would have in the vicinity of 60 -- I think it was something like that, 60 to 70 witnesses. And the fact that two of the trials that I'm familiar with, the Srebrenica trial and the Kvocka trial, have had respectively in the vicinity of 50 and 65 witnesses and the Prosecution has been held to approximately 12 trial weeks, meaning five trial days. 12 weeks in one case, I think 13 in the other. I see no reason, looking at the indictment here and looking at the list of facts that the Prosecution intends to prove, why this trial should be more prolonged than that. So I would -- I am estimating, in my own mind, that the trial would be capable of being performed in, and I think this is even being somewhat generous, approximately 12 weeks' time for the Prosecution and a proportionate time for the Defence, which would bring us within the Tribunal's aim of completing trials somewhere in the vicinity of six months. At least that's the aim that I'm looking forward to, and I hope that both sides will do their best to come within that. Now, having made those preliminary statements, let me go over and find out where we are with regard to some of the matters that I laid down in the Scheduling Order. In the first case, I'd like to find out whether we're done now with the disclosure of witness statements, insofar as the Prosecution knows who the witnesses -- accepting the fact that in every case there may be later revelations of new witnesses. As of the last Status Conference, the Prosecutor said all but 34 of the statements had been translated into B/C/S and disclosed to both of the defendants' counsel, and the rest would be disclosed by mid-August. Now, has that been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, by the 14th of September, which is today, we have disclosed, in total, 319 witness statements in B/C/S to both Defence councils. These statements were taken from 125 witnesses by the OTP investigators. We also disclosed the witness statements taken by the local authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Germany, and Denmark. 123 witnesses were interviewed more than once, and all these witness statements were also disclosed to the Defence. We also disclosed to the Defence all names of the witnesses we intend to call to the trial. We also disclosed the full statement of the autopsy expert, Mr. Dobraca, whom the Prosecutor tends to call to the court. And also we disclose to the Defence Professor Pajic, the witness statement, who will be called to the court as an expert witness on international law matters which may arise during the trial. Colin Kaiser reports of testimony in the Blaskic case were also disclosed to the Defence because the Prosecutors plan to call him as an expert witness on cultural and religious heritage, and crimes aimed against these issues. Eleven witness statements, six from English and five from German, are still to be translated into B/C/S. Unfortunately, the Translation Unit has not met our deadline for the translation of all 29 witness statements we had at our previous Status Conference. From five witness statements in German, we had expected to be translated by the middle of August. Five only were translated into English, and now five, these witness statements, are awaiting translation into B/C/S. I suppose that all this work should be done by the end of September, and then we will disclose all the witness statements to the Defence. That will be all the witness statements we have so far at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So let me make sure I have your bottom line. Your bottom line is that there are how many yet to be disclosed which you fully expect to be disclosed to the defendants, in B/C/S, by the end of September? How many are outstanding that haven't been disclosed yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Eleven in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You fully expect those to be done by the end of September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUWKNECHT
utterances.text: I do hope that this job will be done by the Translation Unit. At least now the Translation Unit is here -- I mean, all the staff is almost available. And so, there are reasons to expect that all these jobs will be done by the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krsnik, is that in accord with your experience? Do you have all the statements except for the ones which he's talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 26th July we received 204 witness statements. On the 5th September, we received an additional 120 statements, and we also received three expert statements from the Kupreskic, Kovacevic, Kordic trials which we had requested, at that meeting, they were given to us. So in total, we received 424 witness statements and an additional three have been announced by our learned friends in a meeting which we held on the 5th of September, as still forthcoming. In fact, my apologies, I believe that we have just received them. I'm referring to the three witnesses. But we need to verify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can confirm -- I'll be very brief -- everything that my learned friend from the Prosecution has said is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That sounds pretty good. Now, let me ask you this: If it turns out that you cannot -- that there are more delays, that you cannot finish by the end of September with those statements, will you let me know as the Pre-Trial Judge so that I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If their not disclosed by the end of September. Thank you. The second item is just a pro forma one. It is just reminding the Prosecutor of their continuing duties under Rule 68 to disclose exculpatory evidence. I'm sure that that reminder is unnecessary, but I make it nonetheless. Now, you alluded very briefly to the expert reports too, and I just want to confirm that. At the last Status Conference, you said that you'd informally disclosed the autopsy expert report to the Defence and was waiting for the translation of the relevant portions on destruction of religious and cultural institutions. Now, do I understand from what you just said a few minutes ago that that translation has been completed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. And the Prosecution, you mentioned another one, another expert report; namely, was it the international law expert report. Now, those reports, do you have a time when you think they'll be formally filed with the Chamber so that the time begins to run for the Defence to decide whether or not they want to cross-examine the experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: As soon as we have the date of the trial, we'll file all these reports to the Judge or the Trial Chamber, so we'll comply with our obligation under Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, at the last Status Conference, the Prosecution indicated that it was considering, and I've invited additionally today your consideration, of possible notice of -- to take judicial notice of documentary evidence in other cases and, where appropriate, adjudicated facts on that. I want to elaborate on that a little bit. At our last Status Conference -- before the last Status Conference, we did receive what I then said I found to be a very helpful submission of the Prosecution as to the facts that it intended to prove at trial, along with the summaries of all potential witnesses known at that time and what they would testify about. Now, I asked you at that time, Mr. Krsnik, to go through the facts and to see if there were some that you could admit. Mr. Seric did that in the case of Mr. Martinovic. I understand from the Prosecution's subsequent filing that you were not able to or did not find that there were any of those facts that you could admit; is that true? In other words, can I understand from you that you've reached a point where you are not going to say that you will not dispute any of those 186 facts that were listed by the Prosecution? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Naletilic maintains the position which it submitted at all other Status Conferences, and that reflects the position of our client. I will repeat what I have stated in the last Status Conference. Unfortunately, this was supported by the events of the last two days in Croatia. I don't know if I can mention the name of a person which was mentioned before then; it was redacted from the transcript. I believe that we all know who it is. He was just arrested in Zagreb, and there are some very controversial facts that have come out in relation to that. The Prosecutor is saying that it was not on orders of the Tribunal in The Hague, and then there are those who claim otherwise. We still don't know whether this was done after some statements of Mr. Naletilic, and because of all this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I simply wanted to say, Mr. Krsnik, that I don't want to get into the merits of any of these fact-findings. I was asking you because I was somewhat surprised. There are many facts in there, and I actually stated in the Scheduling Order the numberings of many of them, which I don't think -- it's very difficult to relate them to anything specifically going on in Croatia now, or even in the recent past. I gave you an example at the last Status Conference, things like when particular countries were officially recognised, et cetera. I'm just trying to ascertain your position now. You say you're not willing to concede any of those, and so if that's true - as I said before, you can lead a horse to water but you can't make him drink - we can simply invite the Prosecution to see if some of those facts are amenable to judicial notice, to use of transcripts from other proceedings, to affidavits, to other ways in which we can go ahead with the trial. But that is your present position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my present position, Your Honour. We had very comprehensive discussions with our learned friends from the Prosecution, and indeed we did negotiate on everything. But the position of the Defence is that so long as we don't see that the indictment is the final one, and this is the indictment that is going to be used at trial, anything that can be detrimental to my client, my client has stated that he is -- did not plead guilty on any of the charges. He does not feel guilty on any count, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We seem to be talking about two different things, Mr. Krsnik. I understand your client has not pleaded guilty to anything, and I'm not even talking so much about any allegations in the indictment now. We're just talking about the many subsidiaries levels of facts that will come out at trial one way or another. If you don't admit any of those facts, then they will be proven by expedited means where appropriate. Otherwise, I think one thing that we're determined here, I'm sure the Prosecution, and I'm sure it's in your client's interest as well, is that we get to trial, one, as quickly as we can; two, that we have a fair but an expeditious trial. And we will do that. So I don't know whether at a certain point, when the Prosecution puts in its pre-trial briefs under 65 ter, the Rules require that you, a few weeks later, put in your brief in which you pinpoint everything that you dispute and give the reasons why. So I assume that you're willing to follow the Rules and will do that in due course. We also discussed last time the possibility of depositions, and both sides seemed willing to have some depositions at which there would be a Presiding Officer and your clients could be present if they wished to be present. Have you made any progress on those? Let me ask Mr. Terrier first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. With your permission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief reply. I absolutely agree with you that the only fair trial is an expeditious one and an effective one. We're not here to obstruct the work of the Court. The Defence is only mindful of the fact that if it did not dispute the facts that were raised by the Prosecution this trial would not be necessary. Let me just give you a very quick example in reply to the recognition of the Republic of Croatia. When we are absolutely certain that the Prosecution has completed their part of work - because as you know conflicts were there even before the recognition of the Croatian sovereignty, and this is why the Defence is abundantly cautious - I believe that later on we will be able to stipulate certain facts. So this is not my final position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear it's not your final position, but meanwhile our preparations must go on. So I'm simply advising you that when we do get the Prosecution's submission, either as a pre-trial brief you will be required under the Rules to give us some reasons for disputing anything. And should they make motions for judicial notice, again you'll have an opportunity to, but also a responsibility to tell us why you don't think some of those should go ahead and be granted. I have your position, Mr. Krsnik. Go ahead, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will be prepared for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, on depositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, about the depositions. During the working meeting we had with Defence counsel, and as Mr. Krsnik said earlier on it was a very fruitful meeting, during that meeting, Defence counsel admitted the principle of Rule 71 depositions with a Presiding Officer. I think that's a very positive step for the rest of this trial, because we indeed believe that for a number of witnesses we can use that procedure with cross-examination by the Defence and with both accused being present, as was the wish of Defence counsel. Now we are going to prepare a list of witnesses for whom we think we could use that procedure, and we will submit that list to yourself, Your Honour, as well as to Defence counsel, and we will ask for your approval of this list of witnesses. That's the state of affairs. And we believe that this list will be completed very shortly, as quickly as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible. If you allow me, Your Honour, I would just like to add one thing following what Mr. Krsnik said about a number of events that took place outside of this Tribunal. Mr. Krsnik was worried about a number of modifications that the Office of the Prosecutor could put in the indictments. Based on the information we have at the moment, we do not contemplate any modification of charges against Mladen Naletilic; we are not contemplating adding or removing charges against Mladen Naletilic. What I am saying is related to Mladen Naletilic and no one else. It also has nothing to do with the evidence the Prosecutor will offer during the rest of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that elaboration. Let me ask both Mr. Krsnik and Mr. Seric if they have anything to add to what Mr. Terrier has said about depositions. Are you in accord with what he said? First Mr. Krsnik and then Mr. Seric. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle I agree. We exhaustively discussed this, those witnesses which the Prosecutor -- of course, it's their witnesses -- are not deemed very important, will not be important to the Defence, and we will be able to hear them in the contemplated manner. The Defence will only -- perhaps we will organise another meeting for that. But the witnesses which gave depositions before the Presiding Officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina, without the signature of the investigator, will probably be questioned, their authenticity will be questioned by the Defence. But I believe we will be able to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at one of the previous Status Conferences I stated the view of the Defence of Mr. Vinko Martinovic to the effect that we wish every witness to appear here in the courtroom and testify before the entire Trial Chamber, because it is far more important for them to give their testimony here and in such a way so that the Trial Chamber be, indeed, sure of the authenticity and credibility of each such person. But we have also envisaged the possibility, in view of the list of such witnesses, to abandon this position in respect of each of these testimonies, according to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Seric. At the last Status Conference the Prosecution talked about its progress in talking to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the possible procedure for 94 ter affidavits. I don't know whether you have any progress to report on this, whether you intend to use any of these. If you do, I'm sure that you will read with great interest a forthcoming decision of the Court of Appeal of what is required for that. I can't tell you when it's forthcoming but it is forthcoming. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Douglas Stringer for the Prosecutor. On the issue of 94 ter affidavits, there are a couple of points I'd like to make. We have had some discussions with the Bosnian government about how to find ways to enable us to take statements, formal statements, or affidavits in a way that are in greater conformity with the practice in that country, greater conformity than the procedure that we had proposed to the Trial Chamber in our motion. We have had a preliminary discussion with the representative of the Bosnian government about that. I think it is going to be necessary to have at least one or two more formal discussions so that arrangements and potential procedures could be formalised. I think that that can be made to take place fairly soon, although we're not able to control all of the timing on that. It's our intention to file a motion with the Trial Chamber that would embody the procedure that we hope to be proposing, and it's our intention to do that, obviously, before we actually try to take any formal statements so that we know that we have something the Trial Chamber approves of before we actually put the resources into doing that. So it is your intention to do that. Your Honour, whether that motion and another motion that we intend to file can be filed by the 29th of September is a question that I can answer for you. On that issue, as Mr. Terrier informed you, there really is no cause for delay of the schedule that's been proposed by virtue of the fact that now we've got a transition taking place within the trial team. However, in respect of motions, it may be that there is some justification to consider a short-term delay of, say, two weeks or so to enable us to finalise motions, which is frankly, Your Honour, something that we hadn't anticipated having that particular deadline on. We have been working toward a deadline along these lines for other 65 ter documents, but the motions are something that we hadn't fully anticipated. It would be useful if we could consider even just a modest two-week delay in that schedule as to enable us to get those documents finalised. But, yes, there's going to be a motion on 94 ter and it's going to propose a new procedure which we'll be asking the Trial Chamber to approve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, what about -- because I recognise the need for some flexibility on the schedule, but we have to start some place. What about a delay of two weeks until -- that would take us, I think, until up to October 13th by my calculations. Would you request that for just the 94 ter and one other motion, or for all of the motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, certainly it would be for the motions. But I think it would be most useful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To have the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- to get the entire thing pushed back two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That would be good. I think that would be more useful to the Defence to have all of the Prosecution's submissions come in together so that you can get an overall -- even though we have to anticipate that you may send the motion in but you may not get -- some of these motions may have to be decided by the whole Trial Chamber, so you may have an additional -- although I'll try to hurry them along, you may have an additional couple of weeks before you actually get a decision through them. So I actually had that marked in as a tentative. Why don't we now consider that October 13th is your -- I think that's a Friday, isn't it? Okay. That's your deadline for the whole works. Having said that, that would up the Defence's time for their responsive filing, which we had down as the 13th of October, and according two weeks would take us up to October 27th, I think. So you would be asked to give your responsive filing on October 27th rather than the date which is in the Scheduling Order. So we'll take those two dates as now our definitive dates: October 13th for the Prosecution; October 27th for the Defence. I also want to make a note whether or not -- I noted in looking -- this is for the Prosecution. I noted in looking through your witness summaries that you do have, I counted, five, there may be more, witnesses for whom you're going to offer transcripts of their testimony in other proceedings. My question to you at this point is, since you know there have been varying responses and different Tribunal decisions, whether or not you intend to file a motion along with the other motions about the use of those transcripts in order to get a preliminary ruling on that so you know where you stand, and the Defence has a chance to raise whatever objections they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is one of the motions which we intend to file as part of this group, then, on the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, I have one last, very mercifully short lecture to deliver, and that is of course that given the status of this case right now, at least, there will be many live witnesses. You have suggested that you have an approximation, just an approximation, of around -- whether it was 60 or 70. My sincere hope, however, is to ask you when you are doing your 65 ter briefing where you're asked for the first time to put down the approximate times for the witnesses, that you will try to avoid cumulative testimony, and whenever possible pear down the witness' testimony to the critical elements instead of their entire experience. Mr. Stringer, who's been with us in the Kvocka trial, knows that this issue has come up time and time again. Just as an exercise, this is not a formal submission, but I wanted to make a few general comments about your witness list. I actually have a little chart here which is just a work chart, which my assistant at the end of the hearing today will give copies of to all of the counsel. It's simply, as I say, an exercise chart. But your witness list contains 105 witnesses, and I know that you have done right to err on the side of caution in including witnesses who might be called, even if you only plan to call 60 or 70 - I commend that - and it may be that you've erred on the side of caution in stating what paragraphs in the indictment each witness might testify about. But as a result of caution, in reading through, there are many paragraphs in the indictment for which there are an extremely large number of witnesses. Without mentioning them, because it was a sealed document, I will just give the numbers. For example, by my rough count, there are 51 witnesses who might testify about paragraph 7 of the indictment; 22 witnesses for paragraph 9; 46 for paragraph 10 - I have all this down on paper, which I'll give both sides at the end of the hearing - and 73 for paragraph 11. It was very rare that there was a paragraph for which there were fewer than 20 witnesses. So I do think that in preparing for the filing you might think about how you can cut down the trial time not even by calling fewer witnesses but by calling witnesses who can testify about the largest number of things, so that we don't lose a lot of time on the preliminaries with each new witness; and that it isn't necessary that each witness testify about everything they saw and experienced. For instance, going back to Kvocka and using a very obvious example, every witness we have could testify about how bad the food was in the Omarska camp. But after you've heard from the first 10 or 15 witnesses about that, I think the next 40 are somewhat cumulative. It may be that the same thing might happen here. If you take paragraph 30, I think this is a paragraph I can allude to without divulging any confidences, which alleges that there was a KB base on Kalemova Street under the command of Martinovic which Naletilic visited, at which Bosnian Muslim detainees were held, there are 42 witnesses listed to testify about that. I'm not sure we have to hear from all 42 about the existence of that. There is no fixed numerical limit on how many witnesses can testify about a particular fact. Especially with the critical facts like the involvement of the accused, I wouldn't dream of trying to limit you. But I would point out that in many other matters, it's rare that after the twenty-eighth witness we get anything that others didn't. As I say, Ms. Martinez, who is in the back row, will be glad to give you this working chart. It's only for your own benefit. The Defence counsel will also receive copies of it. That's the end of my lecture. I'm sure you get the point on that. The final thing here, I just want to go over again, is the pre-trial filings. So we now have October 13th where the Prosecutor will file the pre-trial brief under 65 ter, and the Defence will be working with the Prosecutor in preparation of their filing on the 27th of October, their responsive brief under 65 ter (F). We also would like to know from the Defence whether - you haven't mentioned it yet, and this includes both Mr. Seric and Mr. Krsnik - whether you plan to offer any special defences pursuant to 67(A)(1)(ii). I'm sure you've been thinking about that. My intent, and I have the endorsement of my Chamber as well, is to have this case ready for trial after a final Pre-Trial Conference sometime in November. I'd like to get the filings first. But everything that can be done to prepare for trial by then should be done - the pre-trial motions filed, the witness lists narrowed to the extent they can, a procedure for depositions and affidavits established - so that the case could go to trial. Now, quite frankly, given Chamber I's current schedule and the two trials presently, it's unlikely that they can take up any new trial until a few months into the next year. But there are at least considerations in the Tribunal that if some other Chamber is able to finish their trials and this trial is ready to go, it is quite possible that this trial could begin then or even sooner. Let me ask if the Prosecution or the Defence, either Mr. Krsnik or Mr. Seric, have anything else that they want to raise at this Pre-Trial Conference. Otherwise, we will wait and see what comes in from the Prosecutor's filing and the Defence filings. Anybody from the Prosecution? Do you have anything else, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one brief thing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because I don't know that your Trial Chamber, or even the Defence, are going to be aware of this until later. But earlier this week we filed a motion which -- earlier this week we filed a motion which, under the Rules, will go to Judge Jorda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, and I -- go ahead and finish, but I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is following up to what we said at the last Status Conference. We've asked Judge Jorda to give us permission to provide the Defence in this case with documents which were submitted in the Blaskic case under seal as part of our submissions on international armed conflict. So hopefully in the near future, if that request is granted, then we'll be in a position to provide the Defence with about 120 documents which we will be tendering into evidence in this case to support the international armed conflict component for Article II. So we'll notify the Trial Chamber and the Defence if that request is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, that decision, of course, is the President's. But I will tell you that I will haunt his Chambers to make sure that it doesn't go unnoticed. Mr. Krsnik, and then Mr. Seric, anything else you want to bring up at this conference? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's precisely what I wanted to raise at the previous Status Conference; that is, according to the instructions of my client, and my client personally wrote a letter to the Prosecutor, Mr. Terrier, precisely because the -- pursuing the expediency of these proceedings. The Prosecutor's Office, the fact that they are preparing their 50 key witnesses -- and my client is preparing by taking the lie detector. My client discussed this with Mr. Terrier and Mr. Terrier answered that he did not accept this. I wanted to raise this again today, if it is possible - as far as I know it is possible according to the Rules of this court - and perhaps if this were to be allowed by this Trial Chamber, we would agree to that mode of questioning as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we, the Chamber -- I was copied with the letter that you wrote to Mr. Terrier, but there is no, to my knowledge, pending motion before the Chamber for any specific procedure that you and your client are contemplating. If you want a ruling from the Chamber, and I think this is a very thorny area into which we're traversing, but if you want a specific ruling, I think you have to file a written motion with the Chamber. That is a ruling which I, as the Pre-Trial Judge, would not feel would be authorised by my decision alone. It would have to be decided by the entire Chamber. So whatever it is, I suggest you would have to formalise it. A letter would not be sufficient on that. Mr. Seric, do you have anything you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nothing in particular for this Status Conference. But I can answer your earlier question. We are not planning any special defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's helpful. I appreciate that. I should also say, though I hoped for even more, I do appreciate the fact that you were able to find some of those list of intended facts that you were able to agree to. So we have our dates for the filings. We will have a final Pre-Trial Conference, it looks like it would be sometime in November now. Let me now take the second purpose of these conferences, and that is to give an opportunity for the accused themselves to tell us if they have any problems which are arising from their current detention. I will begin with you, Mr. Martinovic, since you were the first person -- you've been the longest in detention. Do you have anything you wish to tell us? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Naletilic. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] I have already said it's a B-category hotel, and I repeated this to the journalists who asked me that question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry we can't raise it up to a four-star hotel, but we appreciate your comments anyway. All right. Well in that case, I think we have managed to get out of this Status Conference in an hour, and I want to thank the Prosecution for its -- for its promptness and its willingness to abide by a schedule, even in a time of flexibility. And I'm sure the Defence will be equally cooperative as we go along. And being an eternal optimist, I will retain the hope that as we move along, Mr. Krsnik, you will find it possible for us to shorten the process, without in any way impeding your client's defence. All right. The conference is closed. Thank you. Mr. Martinez is in the back row there and she'll be happy to hand out the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
